dedupe_keys.name: united states municipal experience with pay as you throw pricing national survey of cities with recycling

description: This case study tests whether pay-as-you-throw (PAYT) pricing, which charges households by the amount of waste they set out, changes how much they dispose of and recycle. The authors, at the University of Tennessee, analysed a 1997 national mail survey of municipal solid waste managers and recycling coordinators; the paper is posted on the US Environmental Protection Agency's archived PAYT pages. From 5,044 cities with recycling programmes in 1996, a stratified random sample of 2,096 cities in 44 states was surveyed; about a quarter of responding cities, 250, had a PAYT policy, 188 of them among the 755 with curbside recycling. Coverage is national at city level. The paper is a free PDF from a US government archive; no licence is stated. Caveats: data are self-reported by officials, the survey is old, and cities choosing PAYT may differ from others in ways the controls miss. The study found that cities with PAYT had significantly less waste disposed per household and significantly more material recycled, after controlling for other policies and demographics, supporting PAYT as a tool for waste reduction and disposal cost control. Simulation uses: behavioural response parameters for waste generation and recycling in municipal waste service models. Related records: the Emilia-Romagna PAYT evaluation (case_study-emilia-romagna-pay-as-you-throw-did-evaluation) gives recent European evidence.
